title: The Fast God Chooses
summary: The prophet is told to shout like a ram's horn and expose the sins of a people who seem eager for God, fasting and asking why he does not notice. God answers that on their fast days they exploit their workers and quarrel; the fast he wants is to loosen the chains of injustice, feed the hungry, house the homeless, and clothe the naked. Then their light will break out like the dawn, God will answer when they call, and they will rebuild the ancient ruins; and if they honor the Sabbath as a delight, they will delight in the LORD.
story: Chapter 57 closed with God's promise to dwell with the contrite and heal them. Chapter 58 asks what contrition looks like in practice, and it confronts people who look contrite without being so. The problem here is not open idolatry, as in chapter 57, but religious practice cut off from justice. The chapter develops the call of 56:1 to maintain justice and do what is right, and it sets up the confession of sin in chapter 59. Its promises of light and restoration anticipate the dawn of chapter 60.
historical:
Regular fasting beyond the Day of Atonement developed especially during and after the exile. Zechariah 7:1-7 and 8:19 mention fasts in the fifth and seventh months (and in the fourth and tenth) that commemorated the disasters of Jerusalem's fall, and some people asked whether they should continue now that the temple was being rebuilt. Most scholars read Isaiah 58 against that postexilic setting, when a small, economically strained community in Judah was trying to rebuild and when, as Nehemiah 5 later describes, wealthier Judeans were exploiting poorer ones through debt and forced labor. On the traditional view of authorship, the chapter's critique fits equally the eighth century, when Isaiah condemned worship without justice (Isaiah 1:10-17).

In Jewish practice this chapter, from 57:14 to 58:14, is read in the synagogue as the prophetic reading on the morning of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the most solemn fast of the year.
cultural:
Fasting in Israel meant going without food, and often water, for a day or more, usually from sunrise to sunset or evening to evening. It was accompanied by outward signs of grief and humility: sackcloth (a rough cloth of goat hair), ashes on the head, and bowed posture (verse 5). The law commanded only one fast, on the Day of Atonement, when Israel was to afflict or humble themselves (Leviticus 16:29-31), and the word for humble in verse 3 is the same verb. People also fasted in times of mourning, repentance, or crisis.

The ram's horn (shofar) in verse 1 was a trumpet used to sound alarms, call assemblies, and announce the Day of Atonement and the year of jubilee (Leviticus 25:9). The yoke (verses 6 and 9) was the wooden bar fitted over the necks of oxen, a common image for oppression and forced labor. The Sabbath (verses 13 and 14) was the weekly day of rest commanded in the law, which also protected servants and workers from endless labor (Deuteronomy 5:14).
literary: The chapter is a prophetic dispute. God commands the prophet to cry aloud (verse 1), describes the people's apparent eagerness (verse 2), quotes their complaint (verse 3a), and answers it (verses 3b to 5). Verses 6 and 7 turn the complaint around with two rhetorical questions, each beginning with the words “Isn’t this the fast,” and verses 8 to 12 are a string of conditional promises: if you do this, then your light will break forth. The promises move from personal renewal (light, healing) to communal rebuilding (ancient ruins, broken walls). Verses 13 and 14 add a second condition, about the Sabbath, built on a play on the word delight: those who stop pursuing their own pleasure on God's day will find their delight in God himself.

outline.t: Cry aloud: a people who seem eager for God
Why have we fasted? Fasting while oppressing workers
The fast God chooses: freedom, bread, shelter, clothing
Light like the dawn: repairers of the breach

doctrines.note: Holiness in this chapter cannot be separated from how people treat their workers, the hungry, and the homeless. Religious devotion that ignores injustice is not holiness at all, however intense it appears.

“Then you will call, and the LORD will answer” (verse 9). The people complained that God was not hearing their prayers; the answer is that their treatment of others had stopped their voices from being heard on high (verse 4).

The Sabbath and the fast are both commanded, and neither is dismissed. The chapter insists that their purpose is love for God and neighbor, the same purpose the law itself gives for Sabbath rest (Deuteronomy 5:14-15).

words.note: Tsom, a fast. It appears four times in verses 3 to 6. The people's fasts were real, but God asks whether this is the fast he has chosen. The word itself describes abstinence from food; the chapter's point is that true fasting must also abstain from exploitation and share the food it saves.

Anah, to afflict or humble. The Day of Atonement law commands Israel to humble themselves (Leviticus 16:29), and the people ask why they have humbled themselves and God has not noticed (verse 3). The same verb appears in 53:4 and 53:7 of the Servant who was afflicted. Self-affliction without mercy toward the afflicted is empty.

Oneg, delight, pleasure. Verse 13 calls the Sabbath “a delight,” and verse 14 promises that those who honor it will delight themselves in the LORD. In Jewish tradition the phrase oneg Shabbat, Sabbath delight, comes from this verse and names the joy of the Sabbath day.

christ: Jesus assumed his followers would fast, and warned against doing it for show (Matthew 6:16-18). When he read Isaiah 61 in the synagogue at Nazareth, Luke's text includes a line from this chapter, to set the oppressed free (Luke 4:18, drawing on Isaiah 58:6), so that Jesus announced his mission partly in the words of the fast God chooses. His parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31-46) judges the nations by whether they fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, and clothed the naked, the very acts of verse 7. And Jesus's many conflicts over the Sabbath (for example Mark 2:23-3:6) turned on the same question as verses 13 and 14: what the day is for. The Letter of James makes the chapter's point directly: religion God accepts cares for orphans and widows (James 1:27).
questions: The people in verse 2 seem eager to know God's ways. How can genuine religious interest coexist with blindness to injustice, and where might that be true of you?
Verse 7 warns against turning away from your own flesh and blood. Why do you think the chapter includes family as well as strangers?
What would it look like for your weekly rest to be a delight rather than either a burden or simply time off?
